en.title: In-Process 16th October 2026
en.summary: We’ve got a bumper edition for you this week, with new content for just about everyone! Accessibility Testing with NVDA NV Access Survey New Help Options for NVDA Users Help for Low Vision Users Free Sample Accessibility Testing with NVDA NVDA 2026.3 Beta 5 Accessibility Testing with NVDA NV Access is very pleased to announce… Read More
en.body:
We’ve got a bumper edition for you this week, with new content for just about everyone!

NV Access is very pleased to announce the release of a new training package. Accessibility Testing with NVDA is designed for people using NVDA to test apps and websites for accessibility.

This Accessibility Testing with NVDA package includes: A training module with over 60 topics in nine sections Getting Started Setting up NVDA Reading information Visual Options Keyboard navigation Navigating content with NVDA Working with elements Testing with a screen reader Reporting Issues A printable NVDA Reference Sheet, with the commands most useful for accessibility testing A printable guide to writing accessible content on a single, printable sheet for easy consultation A list of NV Access and external resources and links to further your knowledge A WCAG 2.2 Reference with tips on testing many of the criteria with NVDA A JPG Badge you can proudly display in your email, or on your website or elsewhere to indicate your support

The purchase price of the module is A$250 (+GST for Australian buyers). Not only do you get a wealth of accessibility testing information, the cost of this package also supports the work of NV Access and helps continue our ability to provide the NVDA screen reading software free of charge.

Please note that this package is useable by both sighted and screen reader users. It is aimed at professionals wanting to test websites, documents and programs for accessibility. If you would like to learn to use NVDA from scratch as a blind or low vision screen reader user, please first consider “ Basic Training for NVDA ” or the “ NVDA Productivity Bundle “.

The Accessibility Testing with NVDA module is designed to teach you to incorporate NVDA into your accessibility testing workflow. It is not intended to replace dedicated accessibility testing tools which can give specific information about testing criteria and compliance etc. If you would like more formal training specifically in web accessibility, we recommend Learn.Intopia.digital . Intopia provided feedback on the web accessibility components of this material.

Please head to Accessibility Testing with NVDA to read more and purchase the new package.

Cover image of “Accessibility Testing with NVDA”

The NVDA Satisfaction Survey 2026 is open, but only until early next week.

We are always interested in understanding the satisfaction of our NVDA users, what is important to you & what we can do more effectively. The survey is anonymous & we encourage you to leave comments in your response.

We’re interested in hearing from as many people as possible, so please feel free to pass this on to others.

The survey is short, only three questions – we deliberately do that in order to make it less onerous to fill out. The rating is a simple, and industry standard metric (a “net promoter score”) we can use to benchmark broadly how well we are doing compared to previous years. We leave room for you to add your own thoughts, so you can give feedback on that one specific point on your mind. If you want a response, please do include your email address as we don’t otherwise collect contact details.

We do sometimes get questions like “It would be great if NVDA had feature X” and it’s frustrating to not be able to reply, especially when NVDA does in fact have feature X, but we have no way to reach the person to share that with them. We have also been asked “Why don’t you ask more questions about X, Y, or Z?” – which is a great question. This survey is designed to collect feedback on everything overall, and we try to keep it fairly consistent from year to year. We do conduct specific surveys from time to time, both more formally, and occasionally just a simple question on Mastodon asking, “What do you think about …”. We like to think we are approachable and easy to get in contact with, so do please always reach out if there is something you’d like to give feedback on or to ask.

Please do head over to https://www.nvaccess.org/survey2026 and fill out the survey if you haven’t already.

We are always looking for ways to help users and make more information available, and easy to find. For many years, the navbar of the NV Access website has had a “Get Help” option. This has linked to a single page of really useful information for NVDA users , including the training material, user groups, how to report an issue or get extra voices, and an FAQ. Now, we have expanded it to a menu. The first item lets you get help for “NVDA Users” and is the original “Get Help” item.

There are also several new options, which are covered below:

With the release of the magnifier in NVDA 2026.2, it seemed a good time to collate some of the features and settings in NVDA which can be useful for low vision users. The way low vision users will have NVDA setup may be different to how a totally blind user who does not use the screen may have it setup. This “ Get Help for Low Vision Users ” page includes information about: The magnifier: including a demo video, list of keystrokes, and link to the comparison with Windows Magnifier we did here in In-Process. Visual Highlighter: How to turn it on and just what the different colours mean. How to reduce speech: Turning on or off individual elements, or adjusting the speech mode overall. Working on the Web: Tips for navigating web pages, and copying information from the web. Other Windows Settings: Suggestions for other Windows settings which can be useful for low vision users.

To go with the brand-new Accessibility Testing with NVDA package , we have made a free sample of the material available. This extensive sample is full of web accessibility tips and tricks with the world’s favourite free screen reader, and is still only a small taste of the full product.

Do check out the Accessibility Testing with NVDA sample page in the new revamped “Get Help” menu. If you find it useful, you will find even more in the full Accessibility Testing with NVDA package , plus you will be supporting us to keep NVDA available for free to everyone who can use it.

Once again, our thanks to Intopia.Digital for their ongoing support of NV Access.

Finally, this week, we’re now up to Beta 5 of NVDA 2026.3 . Last In-Process we were up to Beta 2, so here’s what’s been in the latest three updates:

Changes introduced in Beta 5: Updates to translations Added bug fix for NVDA failing to start on Windows versions older than Windows 10 1903

Changes introduced in Beta 4: Updates to translations Added bug fix for lag in the Add-on Store when searching using Chinese characters Minor documentation changes

Changes introduced in Beta 3: Updates to translations Reverted bug fix to terminals, meaning NVDA may freeze again when substantial amounts of text are dumped to the screen. This is due to the bug fix not working correctly Prevented Magnifier crash recovery from flashing to reduce seizure risk

That’s all for this week. It’s not often the latest beta gets bumped to the SIXTH article in the blog! That by no means reflects on its value though – Please do try NVDA 2026.3 Beta 5 if you haven’t already. If you do any web accessibility work, please do check out the new Accessibility Testing with NVDA Package . It will be around release time for NVDA 2026.3 by next edition, so we’ll have more on the new version. And we’ll also cover a bit more for our low vision users as well.

es.title: Un nuevo prototipo busca llevar el Braille electrónico a restaurantes museos y puntos de información
es.summary: Un equipo de estudiantes de Shawnee State University ha desarrollado una línea Braille electrónica actualizable para facilitar el acceso a la información en espacios públicos. El proyecto continúa en desarrollo y sus creadores trabajan para mejorar el dispositivo y reducir sus costes de fabricación. Una línea Braille para consultar información en espacios públicos Dos estudiantes […] La entrada Un nuevo prototipo busca llevar el Braille electrónico a restaurantes museos y puntos de información se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
Un equipo de estudiantes de Shawnee State University ha desarrollado una línea Braille electrónica actualizable para facilitar el acceso a la información en espacios públicos. El proyecto continúa en desarrollo y sus creadores trabajan para mejorar el dispositivo y reducir sus costes de fabricación.

Dos estudiantes de Ingeniería Informática y Tecnologías de Computación de Shawnee State University, en Estados Unidos, han creado un prototipo de línea Braille electrónica que podría facilitar el acceso a información en lugares como restaurantes, museos y puntos de información.

Los estudiantes Parker Lauders y Kade Dancy desarrollaron el dispositivo como proyecto final de sus estudios universitarios. Su objetivo es ofrecer una alternativa a los materiales en Braille impresos, especialmente en espacios donde la información cambia con frecuencia.

La propuesta utiliza tecnología Braille actualizable. En lugar de recurrir a textos impresos de forma permanente, el dispositivo emplea puntos mecánicos que suben y bajan para representar diferentes caracteres. Así, el contenido puede modificarse electrónicamente sin tener que producir un nuevo material en relieve cada vez que cambia la información.

Uno de los ejemplos que plantean sus creadores es el de los restaurantes. Los menús pueden cambiar varias veces al año, por lo que mantenerlos disponibles en Braille requiere actualizar e imprimir nuevos materiales.

Con una pantalla electrónica como esta, el establecimiento podría cargar el contenido actualizado en el dispositivo. De este modo, las personas ciegas podrían consultar la información en Braille sin depender exclusivamente de cartas impresas que pueden quedarse desactualizadas.

La misma idea podría aplicarse a museos, quioscos informativos y otros espacios públicos en los que se ofrecen datos sobre servicios, exposiciones o indicaciones.

El planteamiento busca que la información accesible sea más fácil de mantener y actualizar. No obstante, su utilidad real dependerá de cómo se implemente el sistema en cada entorno y de que el contenido esté disponible en un formato adecuado para las personas usuarias.

La idea surgió cuando Parker Lauders era estudiante de primer año. Tras varios años de formación práctica, él y Kade Dancy consiguieron diseñar, construir y programar un prototipo funcional como parte de su proyecto final.

El trabajo combina componentes electrónicos, programación y piezas mecánicas fabricadas específicamente para el dispositivo. Según la documentación académica del proyecto, el sistema incorpora 20 celdas Braille personalizadas y un microcontrolador STM32.

Aunque el proyecto ha permitido desarrollar y probar distintos componentes del sistema, todavía existen aspectos técnicos que deben mejorarse, especialmente en el mecanismo encargado de accionar los puntos Braille.

Por ello, sus creadores continúan trabajando en el hardware, la funcionalidad y la reducción de los costes de fabricación. También prevén explorar la protección mediante patente y las posibilidades de llevar la tecnología al mercado.

El proyecto se ha presentado en el Capitolio del Estado de Ohio, una oportunidad para mostrar su potencial más allá del entorno universitario.

Por el momento, no se ha anunciado que el dispositivo esté disponible comercialmente . Se trata de un prototipo universitario en fase de desarrollo, no de un producto que pueda comprarse e instalarse actualmente en restaurantes o museos.

Su evolución será interesante para el ámbito de la accesibilidad, ya que plantea una posible forma de facilitar la actualización de información en Braille en espacios públicos.

Si consigue resolver los retos técnicos pendientes y alcanzar un coste de fabricación asumible, podría abrir nuevas posibilidades para que establecimientos y entidades ofrezcan información accesible de manera más flexible.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

en.title: From Word to Teams: Using ZoomText and Fusion Across Your Workday
en.summary: ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech. Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful …
en.body:
ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech.

Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful features of ZoomText and Fusion that will help you be more productive in the workplace. This blog series will run throughout October, with a new post every Thursday featuring helpful information and practical tips to make the most of ZoomText and Fusion as you work.

For many professionals, the workday is a journey through Microsoft Office and a variety of collaboration tools. Whether you’re writing, analyzing data, managing emails, or joining virtual meetings, having ZoomText or Fusion set up to support your workflow can make all the difference. This week, we’ll look at how these tools can help you work more efficiently and comfortably, from your first document to your last video call.

Drafting reports or editing proposals is easier when you can see exactly what you need. With ZoomText, you can quickly adjust your magnification level or switch between different zoom window types—like Lens or Line view—to focus on the text that matters most. For longer documents, AppReader is a helpful feature: just press CAPS LOCK+ALT+A to have the text read aloud, letting you follow along visually or simply listen and rest your eyes.

Fusion users can also take advantage of JAWS navigation commands, such as jumping between headings or moving by paragraph, to quickly scan and organize content. To jump by heading, first turn on Quick Navigation keys by pressing CAPS LOCK+Z , then press H to navigate forward through headings or SHIFT+H to navigate backward. Press P to navigate forward by paragraph and SHIFT+P to navigate backward. Press CAPS LOCK+Z to toggle Quick Navigation keys off again so you can continue editing your document.

Keyboard Echo is another useful feature, giving you spoken feedback as you type, so you can be sure your edits are accurate.

To cycle through the different Keyboard Echo settings, press CAPS LOCK+ALT+K . The setting No Echo disables all keyboard echo. Keys will echo your keystrokes as you type. Words will echo individual words as you type them. And Keys and Words will echo both keystrokes and words as you type.

Spreadsheets can be intimidating, but ZoomText’s magnification tools help you zero in on the data you need. Adjust your zoom to see more or less of your sheet and use Reading Zones to mark important areas—like totals or headers—so you can return to them instantly.

A reading zone is a defined area of an application window that ZoomText can display, speak, or both, at the press of a hotkey. To create a reading zone, press CAPS LOCK+ALT+C , then drag a rectangle over the area of the application window you want the zone to cover. To trigger a reading zone, press CAPS LOCK+ALT+ the zone’s number (1 through 9, or 0 for zone 10).

Fusion users can rely on JAWS table navigation to move efficiently through rows and columns, with commands like CAPS LOCK+C to read the current cell, helping you keep your place in complex data.

Staying on top of emails and appointments is simple with the right tools. AppReader lets you listen to long emails, while Focus Enhancements in ZoomText highlight your current selection, making it easier to track where you are.

AppReader reads documents, web pages, and email aloud while you follow along or rest your eyes. It can read from beginning to end, skim forward and backward, or read just the text you select with the mouse. AppReader reads text aloud in three modes: App View reads directly in the source application without changing your view, Text View reformats the text with your choice of fonts, colors, and magnification for easier reading, and the SpeakIt Tool reads any text on the screen that you select by clicking and dragging. Press CAPS LOCK+ALT+A to launch App View. Press CAPS LOCK+ALT+T to launch Text View. Press CAPS LOCK+ALT+S to launch the SpeakIt Tool.

Focus enhancements highlight the item you are on as you navigate using the Tab and arrow keys through menus, dialogs, and toolbars, making it easy to keep your place. Press CAPS LOCK+F to toggle focus enhancements on and off.

Fusion users can use commands like CTRL+N to create a new message, CTRL+R to reply to a message, or CTRL+F to forward a message. You can also switch to different areas in Outlook with quick shortcuts like CTRL+1 to go to your current mail folder, CTRL+2 to navigate to the calendar, and CTRL+3 to go to Contacts.

Whether you’re building slides or presenting to your team, ZoomText’s flexible magnification ensures you can see every detail. AppReader can read slide content aloud, making it easier to review your work or follow along during a presentation. Fusion users can use the arrow keys with JAWS to navigate slides and read speaker notes, so you’re always prepared and in control. Press F6 in PowerPoint to navigate the different areas of your presentation.

Today’s workplace relies on video conferencing apps like Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and Google Meet. With ZoomText and Fusion, you can adjust your magnification to follow chat messages, participant panels, and shared screens during meetings. AppReader and JAWS speech help you keep up with notifications and chat without missing a beat.

A standout feature for video calls is Face-in-View . Before joining a meeting, open the Face-in-View tool in Fusion by pressing INSERT+SPACE, F , then O . This feature uses your webcam to show you a live preview and provides feedback to help you center your face and check your lighting—so you can join every call looking your best and feeling confident.

Join us next week as we explore how ZoomText and Fusion can help you access more online, making web browsing and digital resources easier and more accessible. Stay tuned for more tips to help you thrive in your workplace!

Have questions? Email training@vispero.com .

With the right setup and a few helpful features, ZoomText and Fusion can empower you to work smarter and more comfortably, every step of the way.

en.title: Decant: Color Sort Puzzle
en.summary: Pour a little color. Make a little order. Decant is a color-sort puzzle with luminous glass vessels and a simple goal: leave each filled vessel with just one color. Tap a vessel, choose a matching color or an empty space, and pour the top group. Two spare vessels give you room to think—not a shortcut to buy. NO ADS. ROOM TO PLAY. - 180 puzzles across four difficulty levels, each checked for a solution. - A fresh, always-free Daily, with the same ranked board and rules for everyone. - Practice puzzles generated and checked before you play. - Satisfying glass pours—or instant pours when you prefer to skip the animation. - Liquid symbols, a high-contrast palette, and sound, haptic, handedness, and motion controls. - Free restarts. No lives, energy, timers, or extra vessels for sale. Find a solution, then try to make it cleaner. A Perfect clear uses the fewest possible pours. Older archived Daily puzzles may show a Target instead; that is a reference solution, not a promise of the minimum. START FREE. UNLOCK MORE IF YOU LIKE. The first 30 puzzles, today's Daily, and three practice puzzles per day are free, with three undos per board. The Daily does not count against your practice allowance. es.title: Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3
es.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 5 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3" La entrada Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
es.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 5 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incorpora importantes mejoras de rendimiento, mejoras en los diálogos de NVDA, y entrada expandida por la pantalla táctil. Se han hecho varias mejoras para reducir los retrasos y aumentar el rendimiento. Ahora NVDA recupera y captura más información sobre los controles en segundo plano, mejorando el rendimiento en controles como cuadros combinados y el explorador de archivos. NVDA ya no hace que se rompan el explorador de archivos u otras aplicaciones al cerrarlo o reiniciarlo. NVDA se recupera ahora más rápido cuando una aplicación deja de responder, y ya no se colgará ni inundará el registro con errores en aplicaciones que no responden. En regiones vivas de texto, como las terminales, NVDA ya no se cuelga cuando se vuelcan en pantalla importantes cantidades de texto. Se han añadido menús de contexto y atajos de teclado a los diálogos de perfiles de configuración, gestos de entrada y diccionarios del habla, haciendo que estos diálogos sean más fáciles de usar con el teclado. Ahora también es posible cambiar directamente un gesto existente en el diálogo Gestos de entrada. Se ha modernizado el diálogo que presenta mensajes explorables y ahora soporta mejor cambiar su tamaño, maximizarlo y minimizarlo. Se ha expandido significativamente la entrada por pantalla táctil. Los gestos de dos deslizamientos secuenciales ahora combinan dos deslizamientos en rápida sucesión en un solo gesto, incrementando enormemente la cantidad de gestos asociables. También se soportan ahora los gestos de borde, permitiendo que los gestos que comiencen a 15 mm de cualquier borde de la pantalla se asocien independientemente de los mismos gestos realizados en el centro de la pantalla. Se ha añadido una nueva orden sin asignar para mover el cursor del ratón al centro de la vista ampliada. Se puede usar el OCR de Windows con la lupa o la cortina de pantalla activadas. Se ha actualizado Liblouis con nuevas tablas braille en Elfdaliano, sami, maorí, braille unificado inglés de Nueva Zelanda, y aitiano criollo, una tabla noruega para texto en español, y variantes adicionales de sueco de 6 y 8 puntos. Se ha actualizado Espeak NG añadiendo soporte para liguriano y abkhaz. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.3 beta 5 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es c1d2cc7bc21126a224fdc0733fef5f20adf212d6098fd31863c89f7d05195544. ¡Feliz miércoles!

La entrada Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

en.title: Welcome Home: Apple Announces Updated HomePod Mini, Apple TV, All-New HomeView, and New Home Accessories
en.summary: Apple today announced updated models of the HomePod Mini and Apple TV 4K ; as well as an all-new HomeView smart home hub and a collection of smart home accessories . HomePod Mini 2 Powered by the S10 chip and what Apple calls "advanced computational audio," up to four HomePod Mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers can be paired to create a surround sound experience with the new Apple TV 4K. Siri AI will be available on HomePod Mini 2 with a future software update. It can recognize up to six people in a household, and can use a user's Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad to draw on their personal context. With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod Mini 2 can glow and pulse in sync with the currently playing song. Users can additionally customize the displayed animations to promote a relaxing atmosphere. HomePod Mini 2 features 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets, and 100 percent recycled copper, gold plating, and tin solder in all Apple-designed circuit boards. It can be pre-ordered from Apple starting today in pink, green, blue, white and midnight for US $149, and will begin shipping to customers on Friday, October 30. HomeView HomeView is a smart home hub with a speaker and 7-inch display, which can either be placed on a table or mounted on a wall. It features a variety of Apple apps and widgets on the Home Screen, and allows users to play music, view photos and videos, make and receive FaceTime calls, monitor and control their home, and more using Siri or the touch interface. HomeView can display a generic screen for everyone in the household, or recognize up to six faces to show personalized content for individual users. Apple Silicon and HomeView's speaker array can optimize audio for loudness and bass response at any volume, with tailored profiles for the table-top and wall-mounted models. Siri AI can be used to play media on HomeView, answer general knowledge questions, discuss recipes, and if a user has an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad, draw on their personal context for more helpful responses. Like other Apple Intelligence-capable devices, conversations with Siri AI on HomeView are synced via iCloud and viewable in the Siri app on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS. Changes made to Siri's pace or expressiveness on compatible devices are synced to HomeView. HomeView features a wide variety of watchOS-style faces that can display snippets of information at a glance, a user's photos, or interactive art. With a supported iCloud+ subscription, HomeView can integrate with compatible cameras to recognize people, pets, packages, and vehicles, and can describe captured video using AI. With Sound Recognition, HomeView can alert users to smoke and carbon monoxide detectors on their iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch. Similar to the security and privacy features of other Apple products, data processed by the A18 chip's Secure Exclaves is isolated from the HomeView software and does not leave the device. Users' personal content, like messages and calendar, is only displayed when the user's face is recognized and their iPhone or iPad is present and has been recently unlocked. The wall-mounted HomeView model can optionally be professionally installed. HomeView is made with 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure base and in the enclosure of the wall-mounted model, 100 percent gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed circuit boards, and 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets. It can be pre-ordered from Apple starting today for US $299, and will begin shipping to customers on Friday, November 13. The table-top model is available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray finishes, with the wall-mounted model available in space gray and silver finishes. Apple TV 4K With the A19 chip, Apple claims the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2X faster GPU performance when compared to the previous generation. In addition, a new, dedicated AV1 decoder enables more efficient streaming while using less bandwidth. Continuing on the theme of recent Apple product unveilings, the new Apple TV 4K supports Siri AI for smarter voice interactions. Users can find entertainment and control their smart home with more flexible natural language, and Siri AI's awareness of personal context and onscreen content can be used to answer questions about home events or what's currently playing. Users with an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad will be able to use Siri AI on Apple TV 4K (2nd and 3rd generation). Three far-field microphones on the new Apple TV 4K support Siri hands-free, allowing users to prompt it by saying "Siri" or "Hey Siri," as they do on other Apple devices. The new Siri Remote supports Find My with Precision Finding, which can guide users to the remote's precise location, useful if it, for example, falls between couch cushions. Like other Find My-capable devices, the remote can also play a sound to help users locate it. Similar to other Apple products, data processed by the Secure Exclaves is isolated from tvOS and does not leave the device. The new Apple TV 4K features 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed circuit boards, and 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets. It can be pre-ordered from Apple starting today for US $299, and will begin shipping to customers on Friday, November 13. Home Collection In collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, Apple has launched a collection of smart home accessories, including a lock, doorbell, thermostats, temperature sensors, and indoor and outdoor cameras. These accessories support NFC for one-tap setup on iPhone, and will begin rolling out in December.

Paperback is a fast, fully accessible reader for ebooks, documents and audio books. It opens over twenty formats and speaks sixteen languages.

Opening documents:

Reading and listening:

Paperback has two ways to read a document. In text mode, you read the text with your screen reader. In read aloud mode, Paperback reads the text to you with the voice you pick in Settings, and keeps going in the background and from the lock screen. Switch between them from the More Options menu. Audio books, like DAISY, M4B, and MP3 books, play their own recording instead.

The reading bar:

The bar at the bottom of the screen has, from left to right:

You can also swipe up or down on the play button to move by the navigation unit, without reaching for the previous and next buttons. If that is all you use, the Hide previous and next buttons setting takes them out of your screen reader’s way. The Swipe up moves forward setting picks which way a swipe goes.

More options

The More Options menu is where everything else lives.

Keyboards and headsets:

With a keyboard, the desktop shortcuts for opening books, recent documents, Find, Go To, the table of contents, word count, document info, export, and the sleep timer all work. So do the single-letter keys for moving by heading, page, link, and the rest, and Space plays and pauses. A headset button plays and pauses with one press, moves forward with two, and goes back with three.

en.title: Getting Started: Essential ZoomText and Fusion Features for the Workplace
en.summary: ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech. Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful …
en.body:
ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech.

Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful features of ZoomText and Fusion that will help you be more productive in the workplace. This blog series will run throughout October, with a new post every Thursday featuring helpful information and practical tips to make the most of ZoomText and Fusion as you work. To help you get started, we’ll highlight some of the most important ZoomText and Fusion features that can make your daily work tasks easier and more efficient.

ZoomText and Fusion offer flexible magnification , letting you choose the level that works best for your tasks and environment. You can select from different zoom window types —like full screen, lens, or docked—and even use multiple monitors for expanded workspace. Advanced Smoothing, including xFont and Geometric Smoothing, keeps text and graphics sharp and easy to read at any magnification level.

Color Enhancements allow you to adjust color settings for better clarity. You can apply preset color schemes, switch to two-color modes, or replace specific problem colors to make on-screen content easier to see. These options help reduce eye strain, especially during long workdays.

Focus enhancements help you track your position in menus, dialogs, and application controls, so you never lose your place. Mouse pointers and cursors can be customized in size and color, making them easier to spot and follow on the screen.

AppReader is a built-in tool that reads documents, web pages, and emails aloud, supporting users who need to hear text read aloud. This is extremely useful for users who experience eye fatigue when reading long documents and emails.

For Fusion users, the full JAWS screen reader is included, adding speech and Braille support to all ZoomText magnification features. JAWS features like Say All (which reads from your cursor position), virtual cursor navigation for web pages and applications, and Quick Navigation keys for navigating web pages make workplace tasks more accessible. Fusion lets you switch seamlessly between magnification and speech, depending on your needs.

With ZoomText and Fusion, you can customize your environment to match your vision needs and adjust settings at any time as your tasks change. You can also save your personalized settings, so your preferred setup is always ready whenever you start your work day.

Stay tuned for Week 2, where we’ll explore how to use ZoomText and Fusion across your workday, from Microsoft Word to Teams, to help you stay productive and connected. We’ll discuss important ZoomText and Fusion settings, plus provide tips for navigating workplace apps with more confidence and ease.

Have questions? Email training@vispero.com .

en.title: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Review: I Keep Coming Back to the Pro
en.summary: The last couple years have been big for iPhone. In 2025, Apple introduced two brand new iPhone models: iPhone 16e, an entry-level model with most of the essential components of the more expensive iPhones of its generation; and iPhone Air, the thinnest-ever iPhone to date at the time. This year, Apple announced the iPhone Duo, the company's first-ever foldable iPhone and with it, a whole new form factor and way of using iPhone as we know it. In between the new iPhone models, Apple has, year-by-year, continued the steady evolution of its Pro and Pro Max phones. This year, for the first time, I had the opportunity to review both iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. One of the devices was a review unit on loan from Apple, whilst the other was the phone I purchased for myself. Being able to use both devices, one after the other, gave me a unique opportunity to evaluate them side-by-side, and I have a much deeper appreciation for each model and its strengths (and limitations). And after spending time with each phone, I came away with a surprising and yet inevitable conclusion: while iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are similar, they are very different devices for very different use cases. And only one of them is a device I would routinely recommend for most people. Getting a Feel for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max On the surface, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are almost identical to last year's devices. Cosmic Orange is out in favor of Burgundy and Glacier [light blue], but on the outside at least, not much else has changed. iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max come in Black, Silver, Glacier [light blue], and Burgundy. Both devices have a Super Retina XDR display with Ceramic Shield 2; forged unibody featuring an Apple-designed 7000 series aluminum alloy; and a color-matched glass back with Ceramic Shield. iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display, while the display on iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. (Displays are measured diagonally.) The left edge of the device houses the Volume Buttons. The right edge of the device has the Side Button at the top and the Camera Control towards the bottom. The bottom edge of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max holds the bottom speaker on the left, a USB-C port in the middle, and the microphone on the right. There are three different cameras on the top back of the device, housed in the plateau. The plateau extends across approximately the top third of the back of the device. The back glass feels very similar in texture to the forged unibody. In my hand—that all-important ‘hand-feel’—iPhone 18 Pro feels, as Goldilocks would say, ‘just right’. It is appropriately heavy—‘substantial’—and is neither so big such that holding it one-handed is likely to be difficult for most; nor is it so small that one must compromise on battery life or overall form and function. Whereas iPhone 18 Pro feels ideal for most, iPhone 18 Pro Max is absolutely huge in comparison and almost feels unwieldy. It is heavy in the hand and even heavier in the pocket of my khakis. One-handed usage is not really an option, though if you are already used to and comfortable with the Pro Max phones, do note that iPhone 18 Pro Max has not changed in size. Battery Life iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback with up to 24 hours of typical usage per charge, while iPhone 18 Pro Max offers up to 45 hours of video playback and up to 30 hours of typical usage per charge. In my experience, battery life on even the smaller iPhone 18 Pro has been enough to get me through the day, and then some. On a typical day, I finished with around 40% battery remaining on iPhone 18 Pro and 60% on iPhone 18 Pro Max, give or take. The lowest I got the iPhone 18 Pro was 21% on my very first full day with the device, and the lowest I got the 18 Pro Max was 32% on a day when, unbeknownst to me, screen brightness got set to 100% and Screen Curtain became disabled. Not counting the days when the erroneous settings were a factor, my next-lowest end-of-day battery reading on iPhone 18 Pro Max was 46% after a little over 18 hours off the charger. On one day with exceptionally light usage, I finished at 64% with iPhone 18 Pro and 81% with iPhone 18 Pro Max. Performance iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max both share Apple’s latest and greatest A20 Pro processor and an improved cooling system. While I do not use my phones for processor-intensive work, what I can say is that day-to-day performance of the A20 Pro is as good as you could possibly want it to be. Apps and screens open quickly, and the operating system runs well. VoiceOver—Apple’s built-in screen reader for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision users—responds as soon as I touch the screen. There is no latency whatsoever. When compared to last year’s A19 Pro, in day-to-day device usage, I noticed hardly any difference with this year's A20 Pro in iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The A19 series of processors already ran iOS 27 and VoiceOver exceptionally well, with Apple definitely appearing to have done some serious work to make VoiceOver feel more snappy. Usually, when one installs a new major update, there is a small decrease in VoiceOver responsiveness; this was not the case for me this year running iOS 27 on iPhone 17 Pro Max. (I also tested several of the iOS 27 betas on an iPhone 17e with the regular A19 processor, and my experience was the same.) Given that performance of the A19 Pro was already incredibly good in everyday usage, it should come as no surprise then that this year’s A20 Pro is only nominally better for the same types of work. It is hard to improve on excellent, but companies of course will (and should) try. In terms of device heat, I cannot honestly say that I noticed any huge reduction in heat under load between iPhone 17 Pro Max and this year's models, except on my first couple days with iPhone 18 Pro. Comparing between iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro did anecdotally seem to be more prone to getting warmer quicker, though that extra warmth may have been caused by a particular third-party app. Speakers and Sound When I shared my initial impressions of iPhone 18 Pro ahead of the launch, I wrote about how much I liked the sound from the device’s speaker. My week with the device confirmed my initial experience: whether listening to VoiceOver or music, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro sound full, warm, balanced, and are all around a joy to listen to. iPhone 18 Pro Max is a bit more of a mixed bag. Compared to iPhone 18 Pro, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max have much more bass, more high end, and... Less of the midrange warmth that makes the iPhone 18 Pro sound so good overall. Going from iPhone 18 Pro to iPhone 18 Pro Max, I was, honestly, disappointed. It's not all bad, though. While my primary point of reference for speaker quality is VoiceOver speech and other spoken audio, the very things that make iPhone 18 Pro Max sound so poor with spoken audio are what make it stand out with music. When listening to music, iPhone 18 Pro Max outshines the smaller iPhone 18 Pro: there is more bass, more high end, and certainly more volume. While I wouldn't say that the sound is room-filling by any stretch of the imagination, it is quite loud at close range and more than enough to replace a small Bluetooth speaker. Since updating, I find myself using Siri a lot more for things I would have previously needed to use a third-party description app or AI service for. Asking research-based questions is an obvious one, but it goes beyond that. For example, whilst waiting for the arrival of my Apple Watch Series 12, I asked Siri to tell me where the delivery was on the map. I have also used Siri AI to describe weather graphics posted on Facebook, which is especially helpful as Siri AI can access my contextual information that Apple's Intelligent Image Descriptions or third-party tools cannot. "Where is that line of thunderstorms relative to me?" is a question that Siri AI can answer with access to my location, and I find the descriptions of what's onscreen to be sufficiently detailed and helpful. And yet, Siri AI is not as good as it could be. My experiences using AI services like ChatGPT to vibecode and do other tasks using natural language sometimes left me disappointed with Siri AI. Since Siri AI is integrated right into the operating system, it should be able to do everything that I can accomplish through navigating the UI manually. And so far at least, this has not been the case. Camera, Cellular, and Other Things One of the headline new features of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is the 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture. Being blind, I am not able to speak firsthand to this and, while I had a very interesting discussion with ChatGPT on variable aperture and what this might mean in practical terms, I am not comfortable including any of that here as I cannot independently verify its accuracy. For an in-depth evaluation of the iPhone 18 Pro camera specifically, I recommend this review by PetaPixel's Jaron Schneider. iPhone 18 Pro (specifically) has the Apple C2 modem, and both models have the Apple N1 wireless networking chip. In my speed tests, the only meaningful difference between the C2 modem in iPhone 18 Pro and the modem in iPhone 18 Pro Max was that the C2 on iPhone 18 Pro seemed to deliver upload speeds that were slightly faster. Testing was done on the T-Mobile network in Chicago. As spotted by AppleVis user Zach M, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max support 8-dot braille in Braille Screen Input (BSI), and calibration of braille dots in BSI now works similar to how it is on iPad. Not being familiar with 8-dot braille, I cannot speak to this firsthand. Due to the size of its battery, iPhone 18 Pro Max has a "Prepare to Ship" option that one must use to sufficiently discharge the battery and limit battery capacity prior to shipping it for repair or any other reason. This Apple Support Article has more info. With a compatible adapter, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max can charge up to 50% in 15 minutes. While I do not think I have the prerequisite adapter for this, my own subjective experience is that charging is faster than on last year's model. Which Phone Should I Buy? As I see it, my role as a reviewer is to evaluate a phone and make purchasing recommendations in terms of how I think most people are likely to use it; rather than assessing based on my own preferences which are very specific and unique to me. As such, you may have noticed that up to this point, I have tried to keep my opinions focused on what I feel are the strengths and weaknesses of each device (rather than what "I" like in a phone). This was intentional. My goal in my reviews is to give you information and let you come to your own conclusions. Complicating any attempt at a meaningful recommendation that will withstand the test of time is that we are just beginning the 2026-27 iPhone release cycle, with more releases likely on the way throughout the next six or so months. iPhone Duo is going to be available for preorder next week, with customer availability beginning October 23. The more I learn about and consider iPhone Duo, the more I am realizing that it is going to be unlike anything we have seen before. iPhone Duo is something completely new, with a new form factor and user experience. Watch this space. With all of that in mind, I think that iPhone 18 Pro is likely to be the best iPhone for most people in the 2026-27 cycle. The size of iPhone 18 Pro is 'just right', and the battery will likely get you through the day (if not more). Performance is equally good no matter which model you choose. And while the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max definitely have more bass and high end, iPhone 18 Pro sounds better and more natural overall, and it is the device I would myself prefer to listen to long-term. Of course, there are some people for whom iPhone 18 Pro Max is an easy recommendation. If like me you want the absolute best battery life possible, iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only phone to get. Likewise, iPhone 18 Pro Max is also a strong contender for people with low vision, though the iPhone Duo I think will be the winner in that category with its 7.6-inch inner display. I just would not recommend iPhone 18 Pro Max for someone whose top priority is sound quality of VoiceOver or other spoken audio, or if you value being able to hold and use your device easily in one hand. If you want a new iPhone but the 18 Pro/Max and Duo are not in your budget, consider that Apple has over the last couple years released budget-oriented iPhone models in the early part of the year. If the past couple years are any indicator, these devices will likely include a current-generation A20-series processor, so day-to-day performance will likely be on par with the Pro/Max and Duo for everyday use. When buying a new iPhone, there are a couple of things I would actively caution you against. First, I would not recommend buying an older iPhone model (including the currently available iPhone Air, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17e), as these devices have older processors. While software support on older devices is very good (iOS 27, for example, will run on the 2019 iPhone 11 series), Apple has historically ended software support one processor generation at a time. Put another way: an iPhone 18 is likely to get one more year of software updates than is the iPhone 17 series and original iPhone Air, as these devices have last year's A19-series processors. The other thing I encourage caution with is carrier iPhone promos. While these programs can provide great-looking offers up front, I am of the opinion that carrier promos are primarily meant to benefit the carrier and keep the customer locked in and paying. If buying from your carrier, make sure the math works out and it really is in your best interest. Depending on your location, Apple may offer financing and upgrade options, so you could buy on installments directly from Apple and avoid your carrier entirely. Lastly, if you want a refurbished iPhone, stick to devices certified refurbished by Apple. If you buy a refurbished device from Apple, you are guaranteed a certain level of quality that you may not easily find on the used market. Conclusion On the day I published this review, I did something surprising: I transferred all of my data and my cellular plans back onto iPhone 18 Pro. As much as I love the battery life of iPhone 18 Pro Max, I kept being drawn back to iPhone 18 Pro for its size, form factor, 'holdability', and great-sounding speakers. While my personal preference is and will always be for the phone with the largest battery, iPhone 18 Pro really is, I think, the best iPhone for most people this year. I really do like it.

en.title: Third-Party Screen Readers: Are They a Security Risk?
en.summary: Unlike iOS, Android allows third-party apps to request accessibility permission, which makes it possible to develop screen readers for Android rather than limiting blind users…
en.body:
Published 7 October 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Unlike iOS, Android allows third-party apps to request accessibility permission, which makes it possible to develop screen readers for Android rather than limiting blind users to the built-in screen reader, TalkBack.

The presence of third-party screen readers has helped compensate for the lack of features and responsiveness issues in TalkBack. However, for a screen reader to work, it needs to be granted accessibility permission, which comes with powerful privileges that can pose serious risks if they fall into the wrong hands. The risks that come with granting accessibility permission, as well as the gains it provides, and the balance between security and openness, have been hot topics throughout the years. With the growing popularity of third-party screen readers, including new ones being developed recently with the help of AI-assisted vibe coding, the security aspect is becoming increasingly important to discuss and understand so that users can make informed decisions.

Before going any further, I want to state from the outset that the goal of this article is neither to give clearance to any screen reader or service, nor to accuse another of wrongdoing.

Table of Contents

The following definition is taken directly from the Android Developers website :

“An accessibility service is an app that enhances the user interface to assist users with disabilities or who might temporarily be unable to fully interact with a device. These services run in the background and communicate with the system to inspect screen content and interact with apps on the user’s behalf. Examples include screen readers (like TalkBack), Switch Access tools, and voice control systems.”

An article titled Accessibility Service – An Android Blessing and a Security Challenge in the Same Package from Bitdefender states:

“Android’s accessibility service is a powerful tool that allows people with disabilities to use mobile devices more easily. It’s also a favorite among criminals seeking to take over a device because it holds so much power.”

When granting an app permission to act as an accessibility service, the user gives the app access to powerful capabilities, including:

Although accessibility permission is built for services like screen readers, which are the focus of this article, it is also used by other apps to enable features that would not otherwise be possible. It is a core element of the popular automation app Tasker, and some launchers include an optional accessibility service to gain additional privileges.

Criminals and other bad actors have also found a great opportunity in accessibility services, which they try to seize and exploit to the fullest.

Google did not stay on the sidelines for long, taking active steps to make exploiting accessibility permission harder.

Since 2021, apps that use the AccessibilityService API have been required to provide additional information about their use of the API through Google Play’s accessibility declaration process before approval. Starting with Android 13, apps that are not installed from Google Play cannot simply be granted access to restricted settings, including accessibility access, by enabling the service from Accessibility settings. Instead, the user must first allow restricted settings for the app from its App info page and confirm the choice. Apps installed through some third-party installers can still bypass this step at the time of writing.

Google even restricts the use of unverified accessibility services when Advanced Protection is enabled, a mode intended for users who may face a higher security risk or who place a particularly high priority on privacy and security.

As stated above, granting any app the accessibility permission comes with a lot of privileges. However, in order for a screen reader to work, it must be granted accessibility permission. Without granting it this access, the screen reader is essentially useless, as its core functionality relies on the accessibility service it has.

Despite improvements, TalkBack on Android lacks many features that other screen readers provide. Many users find that third-party screen readers are more responsive compared to TalkBack, which still lags when performing certain tasks, such as scrolling, or on specific devices, especially those with mid-range or low-end processors. In fact, better responsiveness is an advantage that most developers of other screen readers use to advertise their apps.

No matter how we phrase it, granting any app accessibility service privileges poses a potential risk, even if the app is blocked from accessing the internet. However, this doesn’t mean that the app is really a risk, or that it is built with the intention to cause harm or steal users’ data.

The Play Store is the official app distribution store on Android. Apps are required to meet certain criteria to be hosted in the store. Additionally, Google performs security scans and checks to make sure that apps installed through the Play Store are safe. However, Google has its own set of rules that must be obeyed by developers who want their apps to be in the Play Store. If an app breaks any of those rules, it can be rejected from the store or have its approval revoked. Play Store rules are created to protect users, but there are restrictions that some apps cannot meet due to the features of the apps or how they work. There are app developers who decide willingly against submitting their apps to the Play Store, yet their apps can be completely safe, and the source code may be provided for anyone who wants to review it.

On the other hand, not having an app in the Play Store reduces the app’s reach, especially since it is always recommended to install apps from the Play Store as the safer choice for most users. People may also link the absence of a Play Store version to foul play, assuming that something prevents the app from gaining Google’s trust and being listed on the Play Store. As users should be more vigilant with accessibility services, it is understandable when a person refuses to install a screen reader that is not in the Play Store. However, not having a Play Store version does not directly translate to being a suspicious or risky app. There are apps that have functionalities that violate certain store restrictions, or simply apps whose developers don’t like to put their screen reader in the store. They could even opt for an open-source approach that is free from any store limitations, with both the updates and source code directly in the hands of users.

On the contrary, if a screen reader is on the Play Store, that doesn’t mean that it is completely risk-free, even if the risk is minimized. Bad actors are still able to sneak under Google’s verification mechanisms and land on the Play Store, with some apps gaining a high number of installs before being discovered. Additionally, accessibility services that are trusted by the Play Store could be doing shady things indirectly that affect users’ privacy.

It’s worth mentioning here that even if an app is sideloaded, when Play Protect is turned on, which it is by default, Play Protect scans the app for malicious software. If it identifies an app as potentially harmful, it can warn the user, disable or remove the app, or in some cases prevent it from being installed.

In order for a screen reader to be effective, it should work reliably without crashes and should be free of restrictions. Some Android UIs trust TalkBack as the built-in screen reader, giving it certain privileges that are not given to third-party screen readers, even if they are granted accessibility permission. Apps might also provide accessibility UI changes or expose data to TalkBack only, not to third-party screen readers.

For this reason, some screen readers spoof TalkBack by running their service and showing it to the system and other apps as the TalkBack package. Such behavior is not necessarily wrongdoing, even though an app generally shouldn’t try to make other apps believe that it is a different app, if the purpose is simply to enhance usability rather than to gain access to data for suspicious reasons.

Another example is when an app is given the ability to turn on and off other accessibility services. While this is not a straightforward process because it requires issuing ADB commands, it is still doable with the right knowledge. An app with such capability poses a serious risk, and I cannot imagine that it would be considered compliant with Google’s rules. But if the app is built to assist users in toggling between their screen readers, we look at the matter differently.

An example is the Shortcut Menu app, which is available on GitHub as an open-source project, and which I highly doubt could be approved for the Play Store if its developer decided to add it there. The app is built to give users an accessible way to switch between screen readers or to turn on another screen reader if one stops working as intended.

With the widespread use of AI, some screen readers allow the use of online AI services to describe content or perform OCR. They could also allow the use of non-AI services, such as translation or OCR. It is important to differentiate between the screen reader and the services it connects to. Third-party services are governed by the rules of the operators of those services, not by the screen reader utilizing them. This doesn’t mean that the screen reader is completely immune from responsibility. The screen reader should disclose the services it is connecting to, should encrypt data to ensure its safe transfer, should refrain from having any agreements with external services that allow user data to be misused, and should be transparent about everything it does regarding the data it sends.

Google TalkBack uses Gemini, which is also developed by Google, to describe and answer questions about content, but Google reassures users that the data is encrypted and deleted after the descriptions are received. Despite its bad reputation when it comes to user data, Google can be trusted with a matter like this one.

Unfortunately, this level of trust cannot be given to third-party screen readers. Jieshuo Screen Reader, for example, uses an online AI model from vivo to provide descriptions and answer user prompts, but there is no disclosure in the app itself of the exact model used or how the data is communicated. There is also no guarantee that the app would disclose if the AI service being used is changed.

As I am not a user of any other screen reader on the market, I cannot speak about how other screen readers deal with this subject. In all cases, using online services to analyse content should always be optional. If it is not, the user should at least be aware of the functionality that uses the external service so they can decide whether they want to use the screen reader or not.

Here, the advanced extension system found in the Jieshuo Screen Reader comes to mind. It allows users to run Lua scripts, which could be used to communicate with Android APIs, upload and download data from the internet, add, edit, and delete files and folders, and more. Just because the Jieshuo Screen Reader enables the use of Lua extensions doesn’t mean that it is responsible for the damage inflicted by malicious extensions. Users should be vigilant enough to avoid running extensions without trusting their creators, especially since these extensions and tools could be encrypted, so their code cannot be reviewed by the user, even if they have the knowledge to do so, or at least by one of the popular AI services that can review Lua code.

Jieshuo Screen Reader might be the only popular screen reader that allows for advanced extensions on Android, but Windows screen readers have this capability as well. If I am a user of NVDA and I decide to run an untrusted add-on, putting myself at risk, I am responsible for the risks I am knowingly exposing myself to.

With that being said, it is not possible to avoid criticizing how the extension threat is handled by the Jieshuo developer. All users can upload extensions to the Jieshuo servers, where they are discoverable by all Jieshuo users who go to the Extensions, Tools, or Gesture Scheme additional resources. Those codes are not vetted or checked, although their presence on the Jieshuo service could suggest otherwise to an unsuspecting beginner or average user. This user might go ahead and download an extension or tool, trusting its legitimacy, only to fall victim to a malicious one. Jieshuo Screen Reader poses a risk to those users, even if indirectly, because there should be a review of uploaded extensions and tools, or at least a clear warning when downloading those codes that they are not monitored.

They say that humans are the weakest link in cybersecurity, as many attacks are successful because of human error or reckless actions. With screen readers, the role of human error comes into play when installing unverified APKs. If you see a message on Telegram or WhatsApp that a new screen reader has been developed along with its APK, you don’t have to rush to install it. This could be malware waiting to take control of your device and data.

If you find someone posting about a new version of a screen reader you use, you don’t have to install and share this new version with others if you cannot trust the person who posted the APK. Popular screen readers have official places where they can be obtained. There are also reputable websites or channels that share official new versions when they are released.

Jieshuo Screen Reader, for example, is one of the screen readers that is widely shared in groups and channels, with modified versions sometimes being treated as official versions by users who think they are using the legitimate software when they are actually using a modified app. The screen reader has a GitHub page from which its releases can be downloaded, and new versions can also be downloaded through Jieshuo itself. There is also a website, although it is less known due to the lack of communication between the developer and the international user base.

Screen readers that are found on the Play Store are not immune either, as updates released through the Play Store can take more time to be approved and reach devices, and developers sometimes release versions as direct APKs before pushing them to the Play Store. When those APKs are modified and shared as the official versions, users may download them and put themselves at serious potential risk, something that could have been avoided simply by trying to find the official website or the screen reader developer’s channel.

Whenever an app hides some features behind a paywall, crackers try to use their skills to create and distribute pirated copies that allow users to access the Pro features without paying for them.

Putting aside the illegality and unethical nature of using cracked software, using a modified version of an app comes with the risk of malware being injected into it. This risk significantly increases when the app in question is an accessibility service like a screen reader.

The prominent example of a paid screen reader that is widely cracked is the Jieshuo Screen Reader , especially given the not-so-convenient method of purchase it utilizes . Maybe I won’t be exaggerating if I say that modified copies of Jieshuo are more widespread than official copies, with users sometimes even unable to differentiate between legitimate and modified copies. With so many cracked copies available, many users are put at risk of having their data stolen, as well as other damage that could result from running malware included in an accessibility service.

However, the screen reader’s developer cannot be held responsible for what a crack includes. In fact, the original developers are also victims, losing money due to unauthorized access to paid features, as well as suffering reputational damage because of the presence of cracked copies that could cause the original software to be flagged because of them.

A screen reader can monitor your banking activity. It can go further by silently entering data and simulating clicks without you even knowing what is happening, especially since a screen reader can alter the speech you hear or even perform operations without providing any speech feedback at all.

Many banking apps treat third-party accessibility services as potential threats, with some of them blocking them indiscriminately and others only allowing services that come from the Play Store. Others might flag a specific screen reader and refuse to run even if the screen reader is only installed but not running. While the measures banks take to protect users from unauthorized access and transfers are understandable, deciding whether what a bank does is an indication of wrongdoing by a screen reader is a different matter. First, the user must know why the screen reader is denied access and whether this is a measure applied to all third-party screen readers, to those that don’t come from the Play Store, or to a specific screen reader. If users are able to get the necessary information from their banks, something I doubt many banks would provide, their assessment of the security of the screen readers they use would be more objective and not based on assumptions or fear.

In all cases, denying access to banking apps and their data undermines the use of a screen reader, even if the user trusts that screen reader completely. I personally don’t like very strict measures such as blocking access to an app just because another app is present on the phone, since making sure that no unverified accessibility service is running while the user is in the bank’s app should be enough, as the user is free to use a certain screen reader elsewhere.

Some users might be very cautious when it comes to running third-party screen readers, especially those that are not in the Play Store, yet they might have a more relaxed attitude toward other types of apps that deal with sensitive data. TTS engines are one important example. Some people don’t realize that TTS engines can be used as a weapon against them and their security. A TTS engine that suddenly appears in a group or channel is still capable of logging every single character sent to it from other apps, including the screen reader. This data can be uploaded to external services, where it is analysed in search of potentially valuable information. With AI tools that can analyse huge sets of data quickly, going through generated speech output is now an easy task.

If you use TalkBack but have a TTS engine that is constantly consuming an unjustified amount of data, you should be concerned about your security, as the feeling of safety you have may be false.

Another category of apps that is popular these days is online image description and text recognition apps. Those apps connect to an external service, typically an AI one, where the data is sent and analysed to provide the information requested by the user. The number of these apps is increasing quickly, assisted by vibe coding, which makes app development easier than ever. The same points raised about screen readers communicating with external services are valid here, but there is also the fact that some users don’t think about what they are sending to those services through apps that are not considered risky accessibility services.

The previous examples are for apps specifically designed for blind people, but other apps can be security threats without requiring accessibility service access. They pose a risk to both sighted and blind people. For this reason, it is always recommended to check the permissions an app asks for, as well as any suspicious behaviour or unjustified use of a permission, such as access to the microphone or camera, or unusually high data consumption.

Opinions about the use of third-party screen readers differ within the blind community, with people at opposite ends of the spectrum.

On one hand, you find the highly cautious user who thinks that every third-party screen reader is a serious security risk, or even a spy agent harvesting every interaction, and should be avoided at any cost, with some applying this judgment only to screen readers that aren’t on the Play Store. While being reluctant to install potentially risky software is not a problem in itself, the issue starts when those people begin to make unsubstantiated claims. It is fine not to use a piece of software or not to like it, and to give your opinion about the risks of running an unverified accessibility service, but it is not fine to state your own thoughts as facts. Evaluating a software’s security can require procedures that include testing the software in a safe, sandboxed environment to analyse its behaviour and identify anything alarming.

On the other hand, you have the careless user who thinks that everything is safe. This is the user who doesn’t think for a minute before testing a screen reader, no matter where it comes from. This type of user is the one who argues that they don’t have anything to hide and that more cautious people are complicating the uncomplicated. Those users not only risk their own security and privacy, but they also risk the security and privacy of others, as we don’t live in a vacuum. We interact with other people through phones and tablets that could be running infected screen readers, and we connect to networks that could be subject to attacks. Those people increase the risk of data theft, impersonation to facilitate scamming others, and other forms of damage.

As with many other topics, our own subjective judgments play a role in whether we consider a screen reader secure and safe or not. Some people assume that a screen reader developed by someone from a certain country is a dangerous security threat, while one created by someone who resides in a country they trust is considered very safe. While it is true that some countries have better regulations and respect user rights more than others, criminal activities can be carried out anywhere. In fact, sometimes the reputation of a country’s strict laws can be a good cover for a bad actor to gain people’s trust. On the contrary, respect for users’ security and privacy can be found in the work of developers who might live in areas where the laws violate security and privacy. As they say, the person who knows the risk best is the person who has faced the risk.

Our biases are our own affairs that can affect what we trust and what we don’t trust, and it is a wise decision for someone who has escaped a totalitarian country not to use apps that come from developers in the country they ran away from. But we must present our statements as our subjective opinions, not as objective facts, if we are not willing or able to carry out the necessary evaluation procedures to determine what can be considered safe and what cannot.

I don’t have an answer to this question, nor is my goal to provide one. This article is an attempt to correct some misconceptions and raise awareness about accessibility services and what they can do. When you enable the accessibility service of a screen reader, you trust that screen reader, but at the same time, you agree that you are putting yourself under a theoretical risk. Those who follow my articles know that my primary screen reader of choice is Jieshuo , the notorious third-party screen reader. But many would not know that I remained reluctant to install this screen reader for years. Even now, I don’t have the confidence to tell people that this screen reader is completely innocent and safe, despite my personal opinion of it and my use of it.

I still have a tendency not to install new screen readers as soon as they are released, and I generally avoid screen readers that are neither on the Play Store nor open source. When it comes to open-source and closed-source screen readers, I lean toward an open-source screen reader free of Play Store limitations over a closed-source one found in the Play Store, provided I can identify its developers. Although I haven’t tested recent screen readers, I follow a few of them closely, with the possibility of installing them on my devices in the future. This doesn’t imply that I find the screen reader I use more secure than the screen readers I haven’t installed. In fact, the opposite could be true. Yet, I still stick to what I use because I have adapted my usage to the screen reader that I have used for years, without ignoring the possibility that something could go wrong one day.

Screen reader developers should be transparent about what data they collect, which external services they communicate with, and how they communicate with those services. When they offer advanced capabilities such as extensions,they should alert users to the risks of using unverified extensions instead of giving them a false sense of safety by letting them explore unvetted extensions or making it very easy to run extensions without any proper warning.

Whatever comes with the accessibility permission, restricting it is not the solution, as these restrictions cause more harm than they prevent. The solution lies in the hands of users, who should use common sense when they want to install a third-party accessibility service. Look at the gains versus the potential risks. Stay away from APKs from unknown sources, and don’t come near cracks. Keep Play Protect scanning for sideloaded apps enabled. Distinguish between the real risks of a screen reader and human error or recklessness. Look for any red flags, but don’t try to dictate your preferences as established facts.
